_meta.source: derived from the per-trade city economics

verdict.why: Deep demand and a high-earning customer base reward a service trade that carries no stock and turns a chair over all day. Of every pound through the till, more reaches the owner here than in any other storefront trade on this page.
verdict.catch: Space is the constraint, not custom. Prime rent runs near the top of Europe, so the trade only clears where the ticket is large enough to swallow the lease.

lenses.headline: Deep demand, no room.
lenses.read: London gives you customers and talent in abundance and makes you fight for the space to serve them.

scales.label: Demand depth
scales.sub: The spending pool is large and still rising.

scales.label: Talent pool
scales.sub: Hiring is easy; keeping people is the cost.

scales.label: Survival odds
scales.sub: Better than the myth, still no free pass.

scales.label: Room to enter
scales.sub: Most trades are already well served.

scales.label: Affordable space
scales.sub: Prime rent runs near the top of Europe.

income.read: Money runs deep and skews high. The everyday customer earns a comfortable wage, and a long tail above them leaves real room for a premium ticket.

tiers.label: Everyday
tiers.note: The median customer. Values price, but pays for quality and convenience.

tiers.label: Comfortable
tiers.note: The top tenth. Trades up readily; the natural target for a mid-premium trade.

tiers.label: Premium
tiers.note: The top hundredth. A thin, high-ceiling market that pays almost any ticket.

_meta.source: London commercial market, illustrative; no street-level per-sqm held

space.prime_rent_note: Prime space runs near the top of Europe
space.read: Commercial space is the headline cost, and the terms tilt to the landlord. Budget the deposit and a long commitment; the short rent-free window is the only give.
space.peer_read: Against comparable European cities, London's rent sits at the top of the pack.
space.terms_note: Standard on a prime retail unit; secondary streets soften every figure.

owner_runway._identity: runway = (rent_1bed + groceries + transport) x months(weeks_to_breakeven / 52 x 12) = $3,060 x 9 = $27,540 (~$28K)
owner_runway.read: Before the business pays you, you still have to pay to live. Plan the runway from the day you sign to the week the till clears costs.
owner_runway.runway_note: Personal burn only, not the business. Cut it by sharing rent or holding a part-time wage through fit-out.

demand.read: The spending pool is large and still growing. Size is not the constraint here; room and rent are.
demand.note: Annual consumer spend across the metro, modeled. The base is large and growing, not the constraint here.

_meta.source: illustrative monthly demand index; to be researched

demand_calendar.read: A summer hump, then a December peak. The swing is real but gentle; staff and stock for the festive lift, not a crisis.

_meta.source: illustrative opening timeline for a typical storefront trade; to be researched

first_year.read: A typical storefront trade signs, fits out, and opens inside the first quarter, then takes the better part of a year to clear costs. Start the licence before the fit-out, never after.

risks.read: Real risks, but each has a known offset. None is a reason on its own to walk away.

list.label: Rent shock
list.counterweight: Long leases with capped uplifts blunt the worst of it.

list.label: Business rates
list.counterweight: Small-business relief cuts the bill for the smallest units.

list.label: Footfall volatility
list.counterweight: A resident-heavy base steadies the weekly trade.

list.label: Regulation
list.counterweight: Rules are predictable once you know the steps, not arbitrary.

_meta.source: illustrative per-trade city economics; wire to cells on promotion

trades.read: Take-home varies wide by trade, and the busiest trades are not the richest. What you keep matters more than what comes in.
trades.margin_read: Of every pound through the till, only a slim slice reaches the owner; rent and staff take the rest.
trades.easiest_read: The gentlest way in here is also a cheap one, and it happens to lead to the margin leader. Below it, an easier door does not always mean a cheaper build.

_meta.source: derived: keep index = (1 + rev_vs_city_pct/100) / rent_mult x 100, city baseline 100; wire to neighborhood multipliers on promotion

where_to_trade.read: The loudest names take the most revenue and give most of it back in rent; a few quieter districts keep more of every pound.
where_to_trade.keep_note: Keep index, city average = 100. Every inner district here carries above-average rent, so all keep below the city baseline; the best keeper holds the most of each pound.
pro_teaser: Hair & beauty keeps 14% citywide, about 12% in Brixton, 8% in Mayfair
Restaurants keep 7% citywide, about 5% in Camden, 4% in Mayfair
Fitness keeps 12% citywide, about 10% in Hackney, 8% in Soho

locals_intel.title: Business rates ride on top of rent.
locals_intel.detail: Headline rent understates the true cost by roughly a third once rates and service charge are counted. Price all three as one.

locals_intel.title: Footfall is postcode-deep.
locals_intel.detail: Two streets apart can halve trade. Stand outside the unit at the hours you plan to open before you sign.

locals_intel.title: Delivery trades carry road charges.
locals_intel.detail: Congestion and clean-air charges add up fast for anything on wheels. Budget them into the cost base.

character.read: The trading culture here is fast, card-first, and landlord-leaning. Plan for cards not cash, expect a slow first deal, and read every lease as the counterparty's document.

texture.takeaway: Do not plan for cash trade; price the card fees in.
Read the lease as the landlord's document, and negotiate the rent-free.
Licensing is exacting but predictable; start it early.
Suppliers and landlords move fast once trust is set.

peers.read: Against its peers London leads on reach and spend, and pays for it in rent.
